articles.title: John Oliver Embarrasses Trump Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy Over ‘Godawful’ YouTube Reality Show and ‘Real World’ Past
articles.summary: John Oliver is an outspoken fan of reality TV — but not this former “Real World” star. On Sunday’s “Last Week Tonight,” the political pundit took aim squarely at Sean Duffy, President Trump’s Secretary of Transportation and former congressman and “The Real World: Boston” cast member.
body: “What the fuck are you talking about?” exclaimed Oliver. “First, this was supposed to be a road trip — why are we still in your kitchen? Second, is there anything less relatable than a family whose conflict is, how do I tell my daughter she can’t go to Harvard because we did too good of a job raising her?”

Duffy claimed that the show was shot over seven months and that no taxpayer money was used; rather, the show was funded by the independent company Great American Road Trip Inc., which listed 17 sponsors, Boeing, Toyota, Shell and United Airlines among them, all companies overseen and regulated by Duffy’s Department of Transportation.
“That’s not great! The only worse answer to ‘Who paid for this?’ than ‘The American taxpayer’ is ‘a bunch of companies I oversee and regulate,’” cracked Oliver.
And, when Duffy was pressed about the conflict of interest in Congress, he replied, “Don’t you want to celebrate America?” adding, “It’s our birthday!”

articles.title: ‘Boorman and the Devil’ Review: The Making of John Boorman’s 1977 Disaster ‘Exorcist II: The Heretic’ Becomes a Documentary So Unbelievable It’s Funny
articles.summary: You might call Boorman’s fortitude admirable, but you could also call it delusional. And it lends "Boorman and the Devil" the quality of a true-life Christopher Guest movie.
body: John Boorman admits that his "Exorcist" sequel is one of the most infamous debacles of the '70s. But he still doesn't seem to know why.

Here’s the thing about synchronized hypnosis. It’s one of those fruit-loop 1970s ideas — but more than that, it proved to be uniquely static as drama. “Exorcist II” turned out to be a movie about people sitting in a room staring at each other with wiry metal headbands on.

I saw “Exorcist II: The Heretic” the week it came out, and from the moment Linda Blair appeared, doing a smiley tap-dance for no good reason, through the orgy-of-destruction climax in what looked like a discotheque from hell, the film was staggering in its ineptitude. I left the theater shaking my head in disbelief. I had never seen it again until a year ago, and was unsurprised to discover that time had not been kind to it.
points: You might call Boorman’s fortitude admirable, but you could also call it delusional.
And it lends "Boorman and the Devil" the quality of a true-life Christopher Guest movie.

articles.title: Shelley Fabares, ‘Coach’ and ‘The Donna Reed Show’ Star, Dies at 82
articles.summary: Shelley Fabares, the star of the classic sitcoms “The Donna Reed Show” and “Coach,” died on Saturday in Los Angeles. She was 82. Fabares’ family said in a statement, “We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday…
body: Fabares also had a brief career as a singer during her time on “The Donna Reed Show,” notching a No.1 hit with her 1961 track “Johnny Angel.” She parlayed her TV fame into a series of teen-centric B-movie romps including opposite Fabian and Tab Hunter in 1964’s “Ride the Wild Surf,” and she co-starred with Elvis Presley in three films, 1965’s “Girl Happy,” 1966’s “Spinout!” and 1967’s “Clambake.”

Some of Fabares’ other TV credits include “The Little People,” “Forever Fernwood,” “The Practice,” “Hello, Larry,” “Highcliffe Manor,” “Fantasy Island,” “One Day at a Time” and “The Love Boat.” She had a key role on one of the most lauded TV movies of the 1970s, ABC’s “Brian’s Song,” starring James Caan and Billy Dee Williams in the true story of the friendship between two NFL players as one of them faces terminal cancer. Fabares played Joy Piccolo, the wife of Caan’s Brian Piccolo.

articles.title: Lanterns Episode 2 Gives Us A Better Version Of An Infamous Marvel Flop
articles.summary: The second episode of HBO's Lanterns TV series gives audiences a much better version of what Marvel tried to do with the disastrous Secret Invasion.
body: Are you afraid... of spoilers? This article discusses major plot details from "Lanterns" Episode 2.

The "Lanterns" series premiere seems to have gone over well with viewers, even with the ending twist that sends shockwaves throughout the rest of the DC Universe, but it's clear that there's more to this story than what first meets the eye. As Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) investigate the mysterious shooting in Rushville, Nebraska, the final moments make it clear that Hal was right all along. This supposedly "terrestrial" event involves aliens, and now it's up to Earth's first Green Lantern and his trainee to figure out what to do next.

Ringing any bells? If this reminds you of Marvel's "Secret Invasion," well, you're not alone. The notorious flop may not be the most flattering comparison, but DC is already succeeding where its rival failed.
points: The second episode of HBO's Lanterns TV series gives audiences a much better version of what Marvel tried to do with the disastrous Secret Invasion.

articles.title: Viral 'Cat in the Hat' TikTok trend sparks fun fake videos but also real fear
articles.summary: The social media posts have prompted police forces in Ireland and the UK to issue statements that the images are fake.
body: "He's so scary!" says 16-year-old Skye, recoiling at the mention of the Cat in the Hat.
Viral images purporting to show a life-sized version of the Dr Seuss character on the streets after dark have sparked fear and confusion among teenagers.

The posts, seen by millions, have convinced some young people that the character is real and that they might encounter it, prompting police forces in Ireland and the UK to issue statements confirming that the images and videos are fake.

"I was having a sleepover," Skye elaborates, "but everyone started watching Cat in the Hat videos. It was 3am. I wanted to go home. When I started walking down my friends' driveway, I got totally freaked out that the Cat in the Hat was going to jump out. I had to call my mum to pick me up."

articles.title: Star Trek Owed Its Success To Four Things, According To Isaac Asimov
articles.summary: Isaac Asimov observed four details that seemed to make Star Trek a success, eventually leading to swarms of fans, huge conventions, and an entire franchise.
body: With such an inside track in the "Star Trek" world, Asimov had a lot of personal theories as to why the show was so popular among its fans. Recall that "Star Trek" wasn't a huge success when it was initially on TV from 1966 to 1969, but it became a phenomenon in reruns, eventually leading to the aforementioned "Star Trek" conventions in the early 1970s. Throughout, fans were drawn to the show's diverse cast and its utopian undercurrents, taking place in a world where the characters often spoke openly about ridding themselves of prejudice and where diplomacy was more important than military might.

Because Asimov was at "Star Trek" conventions, he got a close-up look at the fandom and got to know exactly what kind of people they were. In an issue of Cue Magazine, reprinted in the second issue of Starlog in 1976, Asimov laid out the four things that made "Star Trek" popular. In brief, the show was smart, it respected actual science, it was ethical and humane, and it featured sympathetic characters.
points: Isaac Asimov observed four details that seemed to make Star Trek a success, eventually leading to swarms of fans, huge conventions, and an entire franchise.

articles.title: Lanterns Episode 2 Contains A Small Link To The DC Universe's Batman
articles.summary: The second episode of HBO's Lanterns may have planted a Batman connection that could end up paying off later in the DC Universe.
body: Episode 2 sees Stewart and Jordan continue their investigation into Rushville, Nebraska, where it seems aliens are amassing to hunt down a long dormant Manhunter. As revealed by a trailer prior to the show's debut, Manhunters are the villains of "Lanterns." But before we see just how dangerous these synthetic shape-shifting beings actually are, the show is dropping subtle hints about Sheriff Kane being far more important than she seems.

In Episode 2, Jordan wakes up in an eerily abandoned hospital after being shot, and is escorted out by the sheriff. On the way, Jordan asks where she's from. "You don't exactly scream 'Rushville,'" he says, to which Kane replies, "I'm from Gotham. Moved here on a whim." We've yet to see much of Gotham in the DC Universe, and Sheriff Kane is the most significant link to it yet.

articles.title: The 6 Best Miniseries Released Since 2000, Ranked
articles.summary: Miniseries get to do something a regular ongoing show usually can't. They pack it all for you so nicely and tightly right according to your attention span. You get one complete story, from start to finish, without worrying about renewal or stretching things out for another season.

A few of these shows are based on real events, which raises the stakes in a different way, since the writers don't get to invent a happy ending just because the audience wants one. Let’s have a look at the six miniseries that earned their short runtime instead of wasting it.

Naz ( Riz Ahmed ) plays a college kid who has one bad night, ends up charged with murder, and in the end, the prison he got stuck in has changed him into someone almost unrecognizable. Now the viewers do not know whether or not he actually committed the crime. HBO takes its time with every procedural detail, autopsy reports, jury selection, evidence chains, and none of it feels like padding.

John Stone ( John Turturro ), the defense lawyer, deals with a genuinely brutal case of eczema on his feet that he can't stop scratching through the whole show, a small detail that makes him feel more human than most TV lawyers ever get to be. James Gandolfini was originally supposed to play that role before he passed away, which delayed the whole production for years.

articles.title: Lanterns Episode 2 Hints That One Character Could Be Far More Powerful Than Anyone Anticipated
articles.summary: Lanterns Episode 2 gives us a clue as to who the might powerful character on the show might be, or maybe we're overthinking this.
body: In brightest day, in blackest night, no spoilers for "Lanterns" Episode 2 shall escape my sight. Beware!

Grant Morrison's issues with the show's color palette notwithstanding, "Lanterns" is a fantastic TV show. Developed by Chris Mundy, Tom King, and Damon Lindelof, the show is more than just DC's "True Detective," it is an exploration of the cost of being a hero, a superhero story about the strict regiments of the job, and about how the Guardians of the Universe are complete jerks.

Sure, there is reason to worry, particularly in how little the show has dealt with the truly sci-fi concepts of Green Lantern and its vast cosmic universe. There's also the whole Guy Gardner issue of "Lanterns" having to explain how he plays into this universe, but for now, this is a rather entertaining story that expands James Gunn and Peter Safran's DC Universe in thrilling ways.

articles.title: Anna Paquin and Melissa Gilbert Call for Protection of Child Actors After Hayden Panettiere’s Death: “Where Is the Collective Outrage?”
articles.summary: Panettiere, who started working in Hollywood at a young age with roles in 'One Life to Live' and 'Remember the Titans,' among others, died last Sunday at age 36.
body: Anna Paquin, Christy Carlson Romano and Melissa Gilbert are calling on Hollywood to protect child actors following the deaths of Hayden Panettiere, Michelle Trachtenberg and Daveigh Chase.

Panettiere’s death at age 36 last Sunday prompted the three actresses, who were child stars themselves, to take their concerns public. Trachtenberg died at 39 in February 2025, while Chase died in July at age 35.

“RIP HP, MT, DC and too many others. It’s a strange small club we belong to and you are worthy of support no matter how our industry makes us feel,” Paquin continued. “Literally DM me. I believe you and I will stand by your side. You aren’t alone. Let’s have each other’s backs. It might make public disclosure less terrifying.”

The True Blood alum added in a separate post, “One more thing– As an adult I’ve had the pleasure of working on productions where the welfare and mental health of young performers was handled incredibly carefully. Especially around material that was intense. It is possible to holistically look after the kids on set and tell complex and sometimes upsetting stories. It just has to be the top priority of the production.”
